title: Greek Lifting Wisdom
summary: NH draws lifting lessons from ancient Greece: statue proportions as a biological aesthetic standard (Apollonian vs Herculean, with the Farnese Hercules as his ideal), Milo of Croton as progressive overload, Sisyphus as repetition and the meaning of struggle, and Hercules as the male power fantasy pairing brains and brawn.
claims: Greek ideal proportions were mathematical and scaled to the individual's frame, such as wrist size predicting upper-arm size
He believes Greek statues were modelled on real men and that ancient men were far more muscular than today's average
The Greek physique is a biological standard: men read it as masculinity and women as good genes
Two branches of Greek physique: Apollonian (perfect proportion, smaller) and Herculean (thicker waist and limbs, more muscle); he prefers Herculean
The Farnese Hercules, with huge thighs, thick waist and big back, is closer to his ideal than the V-taper statues
Ideals exist to be broken; your subjective physique goal is valid even if it departs from Greek proportions
Milo of Croton carrying a growing calf shows the Greeks understood progressive overload
Old-time lifters understood programming without writing it down; programming principles come from nature
No one invents a programming concept; they are all taken from nature
Daily progressive overload like Milo's is impossible because damage outpaces recovery; you would plateau or get injured
Ancient models were physically active thinkers; Plato's name may mean broad shoulders
Being intelligent isn't enough; stay physically active
Modern people should build passion rather than repress it as the Stoics did
Sisyphus symbolises reps and struggle; following Camus, he finds meaning and even happiness in repeating effort
Lifting replicates the cycle of life; we freely choose our boulder
Endless effort without rest is impossible because recovery can't keep up
Struggle is what makes us grow; embrace challenges rather than dodging them
He recommends Joseph Campbell's The Hero with a Thousand Faces
Male power fantasies are a heritage to embrace, not toxic
Heroes like Hercules used brains more than brawn; you need intelligence and a strong body as its vessel
Glorifying the fat body replaces standards of beauty and should be fought
